motion: Did Jesus rise from the dead?

bridges.description: Establish that Jesus died by crucifixion so that later life would constitute resurrection.
Connect early reports of individual and group appearances, together with sincere proclamation, to resurrection as the explanatory inference.
Argue that the earliest Christian material and relevant Quranic instructions cohere with death and resurrection.
Challenge whether the available evidence establishes that Jesus actually died before the reported later appearances.
Argue that later resurrection narratives developed beyond earlier and less physical forms of vindication.
Present survival followed by divine rescue or ascension as a possible alternative compatible with selected early and Quranic material.

sections.title: Death by crucifixion
sections.rationale: Whether Jesus died is a necessary premise of the affirmative resurrection inference and the principal point challenged by Ally.

sections.title: Early appearances and sincere belief
sections.rationale: The timing, scope and interpretation of reported appearances supply Wood's main positive bridge from death to resurrection.

sections.title: Development of resurrection narratives
sections.rationale: Ally's central historical challenge concerns whether later Gospel detail reliably preserves or expands the earliest proclamation.

sections.title: Quranic interpretation and coherence
sections.rationale: Both speakers use Quranic passages to test whether death, rescue and the surviving Christian message fit the Muslim perspective.

sections.title: Comparative method and alternatives
sections.rationale: The debate repeatedly tests the consistency of critical methods and the scope of the survival-and-ascension alternative.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Jesus's death by crucifixion is supported by diverse ancient reports and by the lethal character of Roman crucifixion.
moves.warrant: Wood cites Christian, Jewish and Roman sources and describes scourging, suspension and a final wound as the normal execution process.
moves.inference: The convergence of reported sources and execution practice is offered to exclude survival and establish the death premise.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span begins with the two stated bases for the death consensus and ends with Wood's historical conclusion, without including the following scholar quotations.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: We have Christian, Jewish and Roman sources reporting Jesus execution
So Jesus death isn't simply a point of Christian doctrine
moves.attributionRationale: The passage is continuous within Wood's opening and matches the locked speaker range.
moves.importanceRationale: Jesus's death is a necessary motion-level premise for resurrection.

burdenContact.rationale: Directly supplies the affirmative's required death premise.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Wood reports that critical and non-Christian scholars treat Jesus's crucifixion and death as historically certain.
moves.warrant: He quotes several named scholars using terms such as indisputable, no doubt and historically certain.
moves.inference: A broad reported consensus is offered as independent support for accepting Jesus's death.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage contains the representative scholar quotations and Wood's explicit consensus inference, ending before he turns to post-death appearances.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Jesus death as a consequence of crucifixion is indisputable
that it's one of the most certain facts of history
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood opening with clear first-person framing of cited evidence.
moves.importanceRationale: The claimed consensus is a principal affirmative basis for the death premise.

burdenContact.rationale: Supports the premise that Jesus was dead before any claimed appearance.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: An early creed preserved in 1 Corinthians reports death, burial, resurrection and appearances within a few years of the crucifixion.
moves.warrant: Wood dates Paul's receipt of the tradition close to the events, quotes its sequence, and lists appearances to Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, the apostles and Paul.
moves.inference: The early timing and multiple named recipients are offered against late-legend explanations and as evidence of post-death appearances.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts when Wood identifies the creed as his key witness source and ends after he distinguishes individual, group, friend and foe appearance claims.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood opening in the locked range; quoted creed is clearly presented as source evidence.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Wood's earliest and most load-bearing appearance evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: Connects early appearance claims to the proposed resurrection explanation.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Group appearances on multiple occasions cannot be explained as individual hallucinations.
moves.warrant: Wood defines hallucination as occurring in one person's mind and contrasts that with the creed's reports of appearances to groups.
moves.inference: He excludes hallucination as an adequate account of the reported appearance pattern.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact span contains the legend and hallucination objections, but the selected claim is bounded by Wood's explicit conclusion excluding those alternatives.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood opening with no handoff or mixed speech.
moves.importanceRationale: It addresses a central alternative explanation for the appearance reports.

burdenContact.rationale: Narrows the explanatory alternatives Wood considers available.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: The apostles' endurance of prison, flogging and death shows that they sincerely believed their resurrection proclamation.
moves.warrant: Wood cites reported persecution of Peter, John, James and Paul and explicitly limits the immediate inference to genuine belief.
moves.inference: Their willingness to suffer is offered against deliberate deception, while supporting sincerity rather than directly proving resurrection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with the deception hypothesis and ends with the quoted historian's qualified statement that the disciples must have experienced something.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood opening; the source qualification is explicit in the selected span.
moves.importanceRationale: Sincerity is a major premise in Wood's inference from testimony to resurrection.

burdenContact.rationale: Supports trust in the witnesses' sincerity without equating sincerity with truth.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Quranic references to true followers becoming uppermost and Christians judging by the Gospel fit followers who proclaimed Jesus's death and resurrection.
moves.warrant: Wood cites Quran 61:14, 7:157 and 5:47 and identifies the historically uppermost Christians and seventh-century Gospel as affirming death and resurrection.
moves.inference: He argues that denying death and resurrection creates an internal Quranic consistency problem.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains Wood's two distinct but linked Quranic consistency claims and ends with their stated contradiction conclusion.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood opening; all Quranic statements are presented as his cited evidence.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies a subsidiary internal critique of the opposing religious framework.

burdenContact.rationale: Argues that Quranic instructions cohere with the affirmative historical account.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: The Quranic denial need not imply substitution, for which Ally sees no historical reason; it can deny that the opponents actually killed Jesus.
moves.warrant: Ally distinguishes being put on a cross from being killed by crucifixion and treats the relevant Quranic phrase as impersonal and compatible with apparent success that fell short of killing.
moves.inference: The Quran can be read consistently with Jesus being placed on the cross yet surviving, without another person replacing him.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with the crucifixion-term distinction, includes Ally's explicit rejection of substitution, and ends with his alternative reading of the Quranic denial.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally opening; substitution is explicitly rejected rather than inferred.
moves.importanceRationale: It defines Ally's actual position and answers Wood's opening attack on substitution.

burdenContact.rationale: Establishes the textual room for survival without adopting substitution.

responseComponents.description: Offers a different Quranic reading under which denial of killing does not require substitution.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: The Gospel details do not establish that Jesus died, and the unusually short time on the cross leaves possible survival.
moves.warrant: Ally cites the reported short duration, Pilate's surprise, and a scholar's statement that crucifixion pierces no vital organ, while disputing whether Wood's graphic details are established for Jesus.
moves.inference: He presents survival and removal alive to the tomb as a possibility that undercuts certainty about death.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span starts with Ally's direct answer to Wood's execution description and ends with his carefully modal conclusion and transition to divine rescue.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally opening and confirmed by the frozen ally-core automated check.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Ally's primary challenge to the motion-level death premise.

burdenContact.rationale: Directly contests whether death before the reported later life has been established.

responseComponents.description: Challenges application of general crucifixion descriptions to Jesus and raises a source-specific survival possibility.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: The Quran permits divine rescue and raising while Muslim interpretations differ over bodily ascent, spiritual ascent and exaltation.
moves.warrant: Ally quotes that God raised Jesus to himself and then expressly surveys several Muslim understandings rather than committing all Muslims to one mechanism.
moves.inference: A broad resurrection-like vindication or ascension claim can be maintained without establishing Christian death-and-return resurrection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with rescue and ascension and ends after Ally completes the material qualification about diverse Muslim readings.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there is this variety of belief among
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally opening with modal qualifications intact.
moves.importanceRationale: It defines the theological scope of Ally's alternative and prevents a false single-view attribution.

burdenContact.rationale: Supplies the divine-raising component of the con alternative.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: Resurrection narratives show an overall developmental trend across the Gospels rather than a strictly linear increase in every feature.
moves.warrant: Ally compares Mark's young man, while allowing he may be an angel, with Matthew's angel and Luke's two angels, then expressly compares the trend to prices that can move up and down.
moves.inference: Later narrative elaboration gives reason to treat later resurrection details cautiously.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact span preserves both the angel qualification and Ally's explicit statement that the proposed evolution is an overall trend rather than a straight line.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally opening with the source-required qualification preserved.
moves.importanceRationale: Narrative development is Ally's central challenge to later resurrection detail.

burdenContact.rationale: Provides the general developmental claim used against later physical narratives.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: Differences over whether the women reported the empty tomb and where appearances occurred indicate substantive narrative development.
moves.warrant: Ally contrasts Mark's women telling nobody with Matthew and Luke expanding the report, and later contrasts Galilee in Matthew with Jerusalem in Luke.
moves.inference: The accounts are presented as shaped by later authors rather than as stable independent reports of one sequence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span captures the complete women-reporting comparison and its stated progression, stopping before dating claims and preserving a coherent, independently assessable example.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally opening with clear comparison of cited Gospel narratives.
moves.importanceRationale: The women-reporting comparison is a concrete major example supporting the development thesis.

burdenContact.rationale: Tests the reliability of later narrative detail that supports resurrection.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: Ally reports a scholarly proposal that an early proclamation involved postmortem vindication or assumption from the tomb rather than emerging, meeting disciples and later ascending.
moves.warrant: He cites Daniel Smith's book and carefully distinguishes immediate assumption from the later physical sequence.
moves.inference: An early vindication belief could precede and differ from later bodily appearance narratives.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with the book identification and ends immediately after Ally states the exact distinction between assumption and later meeting-plus-ascension.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally opening; the claim is explicitly attributed to a scholar rather than asserted as independently verified fact.
moves.importanceRationale: It introduces a distinct alternative interpretation of the earliest vindication material.

burdenContact.rationale: Provides the assumption alternative, distinct from rescue before death.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Quranic language denying that opponents killed Jesus can be consistent with Jesus dying by God's will and being raised to God.
moves.warrant: Wood compares passages in which those slain remain alive with God and in which Allah is the ultimate agent of death.
moves.inference: The disputed Quranic verse need not deny Jesus's death and therefore does not defeat the affirmative premise.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span starts with Wood's alternative Quranic interpretation and ends after he states that death would not prove the opponents victorious.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood rebuttal with cited passages framed as his interpretation.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the Quranic textual basis for the survival alternative.

burdenContact.rationale: Shows a Quran-compatible route to the death premise.

responseComponents.description: Accepts that substitution is not required but argues the same denial language can coexist with death.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: The Quran directs inquiry toward the historically uppermost followers and the Gospel, both of which Wood says affirm death and resurrection.
moves.warrant: Wood argues that the followers who prevailed were death-and-resurrection Christians and cites instructions to judge by or consult earlier scripture.
moves.inference: Those Quranic interpretive routes favor the Christian account over a lost early survival community.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Wood's proposed interpretive method and ends at his conclusion about rejecting the Quran if its named authorities are disregarded.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood rebuttal within the locked speaker range.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Wood's developed internal-coherence reply after Ally rejects substitution.

burdenContact.rationale: Connects Quranic directions to the preserved Christian proclamation.

responseComponents.description: Argues that Quranic interpretive directions favor the historically dominant death-and-resurrection message.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: Psalms used in early Christian preaching describe a person rescued from near death rather than resurrected after death.
moves.warrant: Ally discusses Psalms 16 and 118 in Acts and cites a commentary saying no resurrection doctrine is involved in Psalm 16.
moves.inference: The scriptural patterns invoked by early preaching can be read as support for survival and rescue.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span begins with Ally's turn to Peter's preaching and includes both Psalm examples through his explicit Quran-compatible rescue conclusion.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally rebuttal; commentary and Psalm interpretations are clearly reported as his evidence.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a principal positive argument for rescue before death rather than merely doubt.

burdenContact.rationale: Uses the claimed earliest interpretive context to challenge death and resurrection.

responseComponents.description: Counters Wood's earliest-material argument with a different reading of early scriptural proclamation.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: Becoming uppermost can mean truth before God and ultimate salvation rather than institutional or political dominance.
moves.warrant: Ally distinguishes victory in God's sight from the numerical or historical success of later Christian groups.
moves.inference: The disappearance of a particular early group would not by itself contradict the Quranic promise.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage contains Ally's complete alternative meaning of victory and its afterlife consequence.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally rebuttal with no speaker ambiguity.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers a recurring Quranic consistency objection.

burdenContact.rationale: Protects the con route from the claim that historical dominance refutes it.

responseComponents.description: Disputes Wood's equation of uppermost with historical institutional dominance.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: The command to judge by the Gospel concerns what God revealed within it, not every element of the extant text.
moves.warrant: Ally emphasizes the phrase 'what God has revealed therein' and ties it to his prior examples of textual modification.
moves.inference: The Quran can direct Christians to genuine revelation without endorsing every resurrection narrative detail.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with the Gospel-command objection and ends after Ally states the distinction between original divine material and additions.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally rebuttal and clear first-person response to Wood.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Ally's main answer to Wood's Gospel-consistency argument.

burdenContact.rationale: Allows textual development while retaining a Quranic appeal to earlier revelation.

responseComponents.description: Limits the scope of the Quranic command Wood treats as endorsing the whole Gospel account.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Uncertainty over the precise physiological cause of crucifixion does not imply uncertainty that crucifixion kills.
moves.warrant: Wood lists shock, heart attack and asphyxiation as possible causes depending on position and scourging severity.
moves.inference: The cited medical uncertainty does not support survival in Jesus's case.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span is Wood's complete direct reply to Ally's use of medical uncertainty and ends before he turns to textual evolution.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood second rebuttal.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly defends the motion-level death premise against Ally's central survival possibility.

burdenContact.rationale: Answers the claim that medical uncertainty creates a viable survival inference.

responseComponents.description: Distinguishes uncertainty about mechanism from uncertainty about death.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Raw miracle counts do not show a simple chronological increase, because the earliest Gospel has proportionally more miracles and John has fewer.
moves.warrant: Wood compares reported miracle counts in Mark, Matthew, Luke and John and invokes differing authors and audiences.
moves.inference: Selected differences can reflect emphasis rather than a general embellishment process.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage contains Wood's complete numerical comparison and his alternative explanation based on authors and audiences.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood second rebuttal; the ironic phrasing is clear from the surrounding comparison.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Wood's principal reply to the broad development thesis.

burdenContact.rationale: Challenges the inference that later differences systematically reduce source reliability.

responseComponents.description: Offers a counterexample to a simple numerical embellishment pattern, which Ally later qualifies as non-linear.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Even scholars who date the Gospels late place the creed very early, where it already includes death, burial, raising and numerous appearances.
moves.warrant: Wood returns to the creed's reported dating within months or a few years and contrasts it with Ally's reliance on later Gospel differences.
moves.inference: Later narrative development would not remove the earliest core appearance proclamation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span starts with Wood's explicit return to his opening method and ends with the contrast between earliest creed and later sources.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood rebuttal; the creed is clearly identified as reported source material.
moves.importanceRationale: It protects Wood's central appearance case from the later-development objection.

burdenContact.rationale: Maintains that the core appearance proclamation is earlier than the disputed later narratives.

responseComponents.description: Argues the earliest creed already contains the central resurrection sequence.
Distinguishes later narrative disagreements from the earlier creed's core claims.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: The sources Ally invokes for assumption and Psalm interpretation still explicitly presuppose or proclaim Jesus's death.
moves.warrant: Wood points to the title 'Postmortem Vindication' and quotes Acts 2 saying Jesus was put to death and raised from the dead.
moves.inference: Those sources do not establish rescue before death and cannot bear the survival conclusion Ally places on them.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span includes both linked corrections: the postmortem title and Acts 2's explicit death language, ending at Wood's conclusion.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood rebuttal; opponent and source positions are explicitly marked as reports.
moves.importanceRationale: It addresses the central distinction between postmortem assumption and rescue before death.

burdenContact.rationale: Limits the inferential reach of the con's cited alternative sources.

responseComponents.description: Notes that the cited scholarly proposal is expressly postmortem.
Quotes the same Acts sermon as explicitly affirming death and raising.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: The later Gospels differ materially over Galilee versus Jerusalem appearances and over the physical character of the risen Jesus.
moves.warrant: Ally contrasts Matthew's Galilee setting with Luke's Jerusalem restriction, and Paul's spiritual-body language with Luke's flesh-and-bone and eating-fish depiction.
moves.inference: The physical appearance narratives reflect author-specific development rather than a stable original account.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span preserves the complete geographic example and the linked physicality comparison, both independently assessable aspects of Ally's development reply.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally second rebuttal with source comparisons attributed as his evidence.
moves.importanceRationale: These are Ally's strongest concrete examples of substantive, not merely numerical, development.

burdenContact.rationale: Challenges the reliability of later physical-appearance descriptions.

responseComponents.description: Answers miracle counts with claimed differences in quality, type, geography and physicality.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: Reconstructed pre-Gospel traditions are reported to support assumption from the tomb, while the sign of Jonah is used to suggest rescue alive before death.
moves.warrant: Ally distinguishes Daniel Smith's and related assumption scholarship from Dieter Zeller's further sign-of-Jonah survival inference.
moves.inference: Earlier material may allow divine vindication without the later sequence of bodily meetings followed by ascension.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span begins with Ally's return to the earlier-story project and ends with his explicit quality-and-type answer, preserving the distinction between postmortem assumption and rescue alive.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally second rebuttal; scholarly positions are reported rather than independently endorsed wholesale.
moves.importanceRationale: It is Ally's developed alternative to the physical resurrection narrative.

burdenContact.rationale: Combines, while distinguishing, early assumption and survival-before-death possibilities.

responseComponents.description: Concedes the need to distinguish sources, then invokes separate sign-of-Jonah scholarship for rescue before death.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Critical methods used to reconstruct Christian development should be applied consistently to Islamic source claims.
moves.warrant: Wood asks how similarly skeptical scholars would treat Quranic narratives with reported literary antecedents and later source traditions.
moves.inference: A method that destabilizes the New Testament but would also undermine the Quran cannot selectively ground Ally's alternative.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span is Wood's complete first crossfire question, from the Acts-dating premise through the request for consistent evaluation of Quranic historical claims.
moves.attributionRationale: Locked Wood crossfire range with Ally directly addressed.
moves.importanceRationale: Method consistency is a recurring subsidiary challenge to Ally's source selection.

burdenContact.rationale: Tests whether the con's critical standard is consistently usable.

responseComponents.description: Challenges selective use of skeptical reconstruction against one tradition.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: Ally acknowledges that critical scholars reject Islam too and distinguishes the Quran's instructional use of known stories from a modern historical narrative.
moves.warrant: He says such scholars are skeptical of all faiths and explains that the Quran draws lessons from literature and history rather than presenting itself as detailed chronology.
moves.inference: Their textual findings can be used selectively as historical analysis without adopting their theological skepticism, while Quranic literary reference need not be a claim of fiction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Ally's full crossfire answer, preserving both his concession about scholarship and his stated literary-purpose distinction.
moves.attributionRationale: Locked Ally crossfire range; clear first-person answer.
moves.importanceRationale: It states Ally's methodological qualification and prevents attributing wholesale skepticism or fictionalism to him.

burdenContact.rationale: Defends using critical findings without adopting every conclusion of critical scholars.

responseComponents.description: Accepts that critical methods also challenge Islam but narrows what follows from that concession.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Different authors can report different numbers or details without contradiction, and omission alone does not establish invention.
moves.warrant: Wood uses the example of describing attendance at the debate by naming one or both speakers and identifies the guard argument as an argument from silence.
moves.inference: Selected Gospel omissions do not by themselves prove progressive fabrication.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact crossfire span contains Wood's complete ordinary-reporting analogy and his explicit argument-from-silence objection.
moves.attributionRationale: Locked Wood crossfire range with clear continuity.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers a major inferential step in Ally's development case.

burdenContact.rationale: Defends compatibility of differing source detail.

responseComponents.description: Argues that differing selections and omissions need not entail contradiction or invention.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: The Q and assumption proposal is ongoing scholarship rather than an abandoned isolated speculation.
moves.warrant: Ally cites later work by Daniel Smith and John Kloppenborg and repeats the distinction between assumption from the tomb and later emergence, meetings and ascension.
moves.inference: The alternative has enough scholarly development to merit consideration, though it remains a reconstruction rather than direct source text.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Ally's defense of the pre-Gospel reconstruction and ends after identifying the scholarly lineage and precise assumption claim.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally crossfire; proper-name caption errors are not used in quote candidates.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers the charge that the alternative rests only on fringe, discontinued speculation.

burdenContact.rationale: Supports the scholarly availability of the assumption alternative without treating it as established fact.

responseComponents.description: Defends the relevance and continuing scholarly development of the assumption reconstruction.

moves.speaker: David Wood
moves.claim: Even scholars who accept Gospel development still affirm Jesus's death and the disciples' conviction that he appeared to them.
moves.warrant: Wood distinguishes mainstream development arguments from the further conclusions that Jesus did not die or that no appearance belief existed.
moves.inference: Ally's survival conclusion goes beyond the critical scholarship he invokes and requires a less stable method.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This closing span contains Wood's complete methodological distinction between accepted development and the further denial of death or early appearance belief.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Wood closing in the locked range.
moves.importanceRationale: It consolidates Wood's death and appearance cases while directly challenging the con inference.

burdenContact.rationale: Reasserts the death premise and limits what development evidence is said to overturn.

responseComponents.description: Argues that the cited critical scholarship does not warrant Ally's survival conclusion.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: Ally concedes that critical scholars widely accept Jesus's death but disputes whether their reason establishes death if later physical appearances are taken seriously.
moves.warrant: He identifies embarrassment as their stated basis, notes a reported crucifixion survivor, and conditionally asks how death is known if Jesus later walked, ate and met disciples.
moves.inference: The scholarly consensus is acknowledged but its warrant does not, in Ally's view, eliminate possible survival.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This closing span begins with Ally's explicit concession to widespread scholarly acceptance and ends with his conditional physical-appearance challenge and claimed lack of direct proof.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally closing; concession and conditional argument are both explicit.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Ally's final and most qualified formulation of the dispute over death.

burdenContact.rationale: Concedes consensus while preserving the specific challenge to its evidential warrant.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the reported consensus but contests the grounds and introduces a conditional challenge from physical appearances.

moves.speaker: Shabir Ally
moves.claim: An earlier assumption-from-the-tomb model, together with the sign of Jonah, may fit survival followed by divine raising, but Ally presents the reconstruction conditionally.
moves.warrant: He returns to Daniel Smith for assumption and separately to the sign-of-Jonah argument for rescue alive before death.
moves.inference: The con offers a possible survival-and-ascension account rather than claiming that the sources demonstrate every step.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This final formal span preserves Ally's two distinct scholarly references, their conditional wording, and the closing invitation rather than converting possibility into fact.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Ally closing confirmed by the frozen closing-boundary automated check.
moves.importanceRationale: It states the final con alternative in its properly qualified form.

burdenContact.rationale: Completes the con route with conditional survival and divine raising.

responseComponents.description: Offers a conditional alternative to Wood's resurrection inference while acknowledging the evidential dispute.
